quote: To me, it seems inevitable that the capabilities of intelligent machines will increase not just because of physics but because we're starting to understand better and better how to get those machines to behave intelligently. So it wouldn't surprise me if it happened in my lifetime and I could easily imagine it happening in the lifetime of my children.

Read in full. Ambiguous: target_capability, since "it" refers back to systems more intelligent than humans getting beyond our control, not a named capability; coded superintelligence. Endorsement uncertain: "wouldn't surprise me" and "could easily imagine" are hedges, not a prediction. Agency from his next sentence in the same answer ("the sooner we start solving this problem, the better"), outside the stored quote, so the governance frame rests on context. Same interview: five years ago most AI people would have said human-level AI was "Decades and decades or centuries away", "but now I think it seems as if it's a little bit closer"; and he explains an intelligence explosion as a system at human level that "can redesign itself using better hardware and better algorithms".

notes: basis: "may sometimes be measured not in centuries"; Russell's contribution "Of Myths And Moonshine" to the Edge Reality Club conversation "The Myth of AI" (Jaron Lanier, conversation dated 11.14.14 on the page). Russell's reply is not dated on the page, so year precision only. Read in full at edge.org (fetched with curl). Mentions Rodney Brooks (a panel member) only as the target of the reply. quote: But if that problem is solved — and it's certainly not impossible — then we would see another big increase in machine capabilities. There are two or three problems like that where if all of those were solved, then it's not clear to me that there would be any major obstacle between there and human-level AI.

definition_note: human-level AI
notes: basis: "if all of those were solved, then it's not clear to me that there would be any major obstacle"; Quanta Magazine Q&A by Natalie Wolchover, "Concerns of an Artificial Intelligence Pioneer", dated April 21, 2015 on the page; read in full (fetched with curl). Reprinted by Wired 2015-05-23 (same text, not a separate row). present_capability disputed: just before, he says hierarchical decision making is "one of the missing pieces right now". Same interview: success "would be an enormous thing. 'The biggest event in human history'", earlier "Probably it was just too far away", and he explains the intelligence explosion as machines that "will be able to work on AI just like we do and improve their own capabilities" (he is describing the idea, not endorsing it).

quote: The arrival of AGI, he says, is not imminent, and he won't be drawn on a date: we can't predict when the breakthroughs which will get us there will happen, he insists. But they might not be many decades away.

notes: secondhand; basis: "they might not be many decades away"; Calum Chace's blog report (post dated May 16, 2015) of Russell's public lecture "The Long-Term Future of (Artificial) Intelligence" at the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, Cambridge, on 15 May 2015 (date in the post and in Russell's own media list). The words are the blogger's paraphrase, not a direct quotation; a video of the talk exists (YouTube) but has no transcript, so not checked. Read at calumchace.com (fetched with curl); the page renders "not" and "they" with stray markup inside the words, normalised here. Endorsement uncertain: "might" with a vague horizon, plus an explicit refusal to give a date.

quote: “If we had computers a trillion times faster we wouldn’t have human-level AI; half in jest, one might say we’d just get wrong answers a trillion times sooner,” he says. “What matters are real conceptual and algorithmic breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict.”

timeline_text: breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict
definition_note: human-level AI
notes: Nature news feature by Declan Butler, "A world where everyone has a robot: why 2040 could blow your mind", published 24 February 2016 (date on nature.com); the reporter spoke to Russell, so elicitation interview, primary. nature.com now paywalls the piece; read at the Wayback Machine copy of the free 2016 news page (fetched with curl). Endorsement unexpressed: he rejects a route (raw computing speed) and says the breakthroughs are hard to predict, but does not say whether human-level AI will come (A15 ruling 4).

quote: Solving the safety problem well enough to move forward in AI seems to be feasible but not easy. There are probably decades to plan for the arrival of superintelligent machines. But the problem should not be dismissed out of hand, as it has been by some AI researchers.

timeline_text: There are probably decades to plan for the arrival

The PDF breaks "researchers" across a line with a hyphen; joined here. A14 ruling 11: decades away is accepts; "probably" is not one of the hedges (may, might, could) that make a date uncertain. Agency from "Solving the safety problem ... seems to be feasible". Same article: "Still others think that superintelligent AI will never happen", answered with the Rutherford and Szilard story, which argues against "never".

quote: somewhat more than half (67.5 percent) of Etzioni’s respondents plumped for “more than 25 years” to achieve superintelligence—after all, more than half of Bostrom’s respondents gave dates beyond 25 years for a mere 50 percent probability of achieving mere human-level intelligence. One of us (Russell) responded to Etzioni’s survey with “more than 25 years,”
claim_summary: Co-written reply to Oren Etzioni: Russell reports that he answered Etzioni's 2016 survey on when superintelligence will be achieved with 'more than 25 years'.

The unit is Russell's own survey answer, reported by himself; the survey was Etzioni's 2016 poll of AAAI fellows (published 2016-09-20), so the answer itself was given earlier in 2016; dated here by publication. Elicitation survey (answering a survey item), source_type blog because the source read is the opinion piece. A15 ruling 5: a minimum number of years asserts arrival with a minimum, so accepts with an open high bound; choosing "more than 25 years" rather than "never" supports that, and the piece adds Etzioni's headline "could just as easily have been '75 percent of experts think superintelligent AI is inevitable.'"

quote: The difficulty in predicting such breakthroughs means that giving any precise estimate of the date on which human-level AI will arrive is foolhardy. Nonetheless, most experts believe it is likely to arrive within the present century

notes: Russell's essay "Provably Beneficial Artificial Intelligence", in The Next Step: Exponential Life (BBVA OpenMind, 2017; citation from his own page; PDF metadata 2017-09-14), read in the copy on his Berkeley site through r.jina.ai. The text extraction splits the "ffi" letter group ("di ffi culty"); joined here. The sentence before the quote says more breakthroughs are needed "that we will not know how to describe until we see our best efforts to build general-purpose AI systems failing in interesting ways". present_capability disputed from the sentence just before: "Despite all this progress, we are still far from human-level AI." Same essay, answering the objection "Human-level AI is impossible": the claim "represents a foolhardy bet against human ingenuity"; and "The relevant timescale for human-level AI is less predictable, but of course that means it, like nuclear fission, might arrive considerably sooner than expected."

quote: reading is not yet happening in machines, at least with understanding. But that will happen, and when that happens, very soon afterwards, machines will have read everything that the human race has ever written. ... they'll be able to make better decisions in the real world than we can.

Read in the official TED transcript (page data fetched with curl). Article says "If a typical person can do a mental task with less than one second of thought, we can probably automate it using AI either now or in the near future" (narrow tasks, not coded). Judgment call: "far from" and "much more than" deny that current systems match human intelligence, so present_capability disputed; nothing is said about the future, so endorsement unexpressed (ruling 9).

quote: Since the early days of AI, people have wondered whether AI can ever be conscious or feel emotions. Even though an artificial general intelligence may be centuries away, these are important questions.

The letter is mainly about whether an AI can love or be conscious, which he calls philosophical questions; frame_primary is timeline because the only claim about AGI itself is its timing, and other_concern (consciousness) is present. "may" with "centuries" is a hedge, so uncertain (ruling 10); no number of centuries, so timeline_year blank.

quote: I continue to believe that some combination of learning algorithms, likely yet to be invented, will get us there someday.

Same letter: building AGI is "one of the grandest challenges of our time"; "Obviously, AGI would have extraordinary value"; he co-organized a NIPS 2005 workshop on human-level AI; ends "If you dream of making progress toward AGI yourself, I encourage you to keep dreaming!" Consequences, affect and agency are taken from those lines in the same letter, outside the stored quote; judgment call, so coding_confidence would be medium for those fields.

Same letter, later: "While AGI may be part of an indeterminate future, we have amazing capabilities today" (a hedge, not coded here because it is a separate passage; it would be uncertain).

quote: I believe that most people, including me, currently think of AGI as AI that can carry out any intellectual task that a human can. With this definition, I think we’re still at least decades away from AGI.

No number of decades is given, so timeline_year is left blank and the row is qualitative rather than a range; the lower_bound tag is not used because it needs a year. quote: Even though nontechnical pundits talk about “the race to AGI” as if AGI were a discrete technology to be invented, the reality is that AI technology will progress continuously ... Judgment call: he does not say AGI will never come, only that a declaration of it would be a marketing claim; present_capability disputed reads that as disputing any such claim, endorsement unexpressed.

quote: I look at how complex the training recipes are and how manual AI training and development is today, and there’s no way this is going to take us all the way to AGI just by itself,

quote: Modern AI is a general purpose technology that is enabling many applications, but AI that can do any intellectual tasks that a human can (a popular definition for AGI) is still decades away or longer.

quote: We shouldn’t buy into the inaccurate hype that LLMs are a path to AGI in just a few years, but we also shouldn’t buy into the opposite, also inaccurate hype that they are only demoware.

The claim rejects both a route (language models) and a near date; under A15 ruling 4 a route claim alone would be unexpressed, but here the timing ("in just a few years") is what he calls inaccurate, so coded rejects for that horizon only. No not_by tag because "a few years" gives no year (2025 + a few). He does not say whether AGI comes later (see ng-2025-04, "decades away or longer").

quote: “AGI” has turned into a term of hype rather than a term with a precise meaning. A reasonable definition of AGI is AI that can do any intellectual task that a human can. definition_note: AI that can do any intellectual task that a human can; tested by doing a work task as well as a skilled human (Turing-AGI Test)
notes: The Batch issue 334 (New Year issue) letter, published 2026-01-02; the panel verification's latest statement for him. Same letter: CEOs sometimes assume "AI will be more capable in 1-2 years than any likely reality"; hype risks a bubble; "If we run a Turing-AGI Test competition and every AI system falls short, that will be a good thing!" Consequence (economic, harmful: a bubble) and agency (a test can recalibrate expectations) come from the same letter, outside the stored quote. No position on when AGI arrives, so endorsement unexpressed.

quote: We are closer than before, yet many decades away from an AI that matches human intelligence.

Same interview: he expects robots throughout everyday life within 50 years (not about human-level AI).

quote: Eventually, we will create truly artificial intelligences, with cognition and consciousness recognizably similar to our own. I have no idea how, exactly, this creation will come about. Endorsement: the unit says it will come eventually and not before 2030, so accepts with the hedge in timeline_text (codebook: rejecting a near date while accepting eventual arrival). Same essay: "The singularity will be a period, not an event" and "machines will become gradually more intelligent, generation by generation" (the same capability, not split).

quote: In order for there to be a successful volitional AI, especially one that could be successfully malevolent, it would need a direct understanding of the world ... It is going to take a lot of deep thought and hard work from thousands of scientists and engineers. And, most likely, centuries.

definition_note: volitional or intentional artificially intelligent beings; elsewhere in the essay, human level or super human level intelligence
notes: basis: "It is going to take a lot of deep thought and hard work"; Own essay, first published on the Rethink Robotics blog and reposted on Robohub under his byline; read at Robohub; date from the Robohub byline (11 November 2014). timeline_year left blank: "centuries" gives no number (codebook ruling 11 by analogy with decades). Same essay: "it is a mistake to be worrying about us developing malevolent AI anytime in the next few hundred years" and "Moore's Law applied to this very real technical advance will not by itself bring about human level or super human level intelligence" (a route claim). Target judgment: volitional AI read as broad competence.

quote: The fears of runaway AI systems either conquering humans or making them irrelevant are not even remotely well grounded. Misled by suitcase words, people are making category errors in fungibility of capabilities. These category errors are comparable to seeing more efficient internal combustion engines appearing and jumping to the conclusion that warp drives are just around the corner.

Date: the page gives only the question year 2015, so year precision. elicitation survey because it answers a question put to many contributors; source_type blog is the nearest value for a short signed essay. Ambiguous fields: endorsement and frame. The warp-drive analogy says runaway AI is nowhere near, but the words do not say whether it will ever exist, so endorsement is unexpressed; timeline is present only through the analogy.

quote: "We are going to have more robots, we are going to have more artificial intelligence, but I think people are misinterpreting the progress that is being made," he said. "I don't think we have to worry about that in our lifetime or our children's lifetimes."

timeline_text: 20 years out or decades way ... so far out, we can’t really measure it
notes: basis: "it so far out"; TechCrunch report of his on-stage interview at TechCrunch Disrupt London, published time 2016-12-05 (the outlet's own event, so treated as an interview with direct quotes). Ambiguous field: endorsement ("so far out we can't measure it" says distant without saying it will come; read as acceptance with a long horizon, A14 ruling 11). This is the statement the panel verification used as his earliest.

quote: I'm pretty sure that within the next five years, certainly before the end of the decade, we are going to have not just those capabilities, but those capabilities widely available for very cheap, potentially even in open source,
claim_summary: At Davos: within five years, certainly before the end of the decade, AI able to act like an entrepreneur (a modern Turing test) will be widely and cheaply available.
timeline_text: within the next five years, certainly before the end of the decade
definition_note: modern Turing test: an AI that can act like an entrepreneur, project manager and inventor, and market, make and sell a product for profit
notes: secondhand; basis: "I'm pretty sure that within the next five years"; computed: 2024 + 5 (upper bound); A Business Insider report of his World Economic Forum panel (January 2024), reposted to the LINK mailing list archive (January 2024); month precision. Ambiguous field: target_capability (an "entrepreneur" AI, his proposed test, not AGI as such; the same report says he called the AGI conversation overblown).

quote: I don't want to say I think it's a high probability that it's two years away, but I think within the next five to seven years, since each generation takes 18 to 24 months now, ... The uncertainty around this is so high that any categorical declarations just feel sort of ungrounded to me and over the top,

timeline_text: I think within the next five to seven years ... the uncertainty around this is so high
definition_note: a general-purpose learning system that can perform well across all human-level training environments (as quoted elsewhere)
notes: secondhand; basis: "The uncertainty around this is so high"; computed: 2024 + 5 to 2024 + 7; Business Insider report via AOL (published time 2024-12-10) of his interview on The Verge's Decoder podcast; month precision because the episode day is not given. Ambiguous field: endorsement ("I think within the next five to seven years" leans to acceptance; the uncertainty sentence decides, coded uncertain).

quote: I don’t think I’m skeptical that it’s arriving anytime soon… Soon to me is sometime in the next 10 years.
claim_summary: Not skeptical that AGI is arriving soon; 'soon' to him means sometime in the next ten years.
timeline_text: Soon to me is sometime in the next 10 years
notes: secondhand; basis: "I don’t think I’m skeptical that it’s arriving anytime soon"; computed: 2025 + 10 (upper bound); TheFly via TipRanks (published time 2025-07-21) reporting a Wall Street Journal interview; month precision; the WSJ original was not read.

quote: With the arrival of thinking and [reasoning models](https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/how-far-can-reasoning-models-scale), we’ve crossed an inflection point on the journey towards superintelligence. ... Such a system will have an open-ended ability of “learning to learn”, the ultimate meta skill. It would therefore likely continue improving, going far beyond human-level performance across all conceivable activities.
claim_summary: Essay 'Towards Humanist Superintelligence': reasoning models have crossed an inflection point towards superintelligence, which would keep improving far beyond human performance.
timeline_text: we’ve crossed an inflection point on the journey towards superintelligence
notes: basis: "we’ve crossed an inflection point on the journey towards superintelligence"; His own essay on the Microsoft AI site announcing the MAI Superintelligence Team; month precision (Fortune reported it on 2025-11-06; the page shows no date). The second sentence is about a system "learning to learn" and continuing to improve (self-improvement, recorded in notes only). Same essay: "we reject narratives about a race to AGI". Ambiguous field: endorsement (on a journey, no arrival date).

quote: Yeah, I mean I think achieving human-level performance at most tasks, I wouldn’t say all knowledge tasks. That feels quite likely in the next five years, I think.
claim_summary: Human-level performance at most tasks (not all knowledge tasks) feels quite likely in the next five years.
timeline_text: quite likely in the next five years
notes: basis: "That feels quite likely in the next five years"; computed: 2025 + 5 (upper bound); Silicon Valley Girl podcast with Marina Mogilko, transcript published by The Singju Post, which dates the interview November 14, 2025. Same interview: an autonomous, self-improving superintelligence "should be the anti-goal" (a statement about what to build, not whether it will exist).

quote: As I do at the start of each year, I’ve spent some time reconsidering when I think roughly human level AGI will exist. I’ve again decided to leave it at 2025, but now with a reduced standard deviation of 5 years.
claim_summary: Annual review on his blog: he again puts roughly human-level AGI at 2025, now with a standard deviation of five years.
timeline_text: I've again decided to leave it at 2025, but now with a reduced standard deviation of 5 years
notes: basis: "I’ve again decided to leave it at 2025"; His own blog (vetta.org), post "Tick, tock, tick, tock…" dated 9 February 2009 on the page. Same post: whether the remaining algorithm problems take "2 years or 10 years is hard to guess". The update added to this post on 11 April 2009 is a separate row (legg-2009-02).

quote: Thus if you want the “Shane meta predictor”, then take 2033 as the expected date, perhaps with a standard deviation of 7 years. ... So I suppose that if I had to put money on a date, I should go with 2033.
claim_summary: Update to the same post: correcting for his habit of predicting things too early (about 50% more time), his 'meta prediction' for human-level AGI is 2033, standard deviation about seven years.
timeline_text: take 2033 as the expected date, perhaps with a standard deviation of 7 years ... I should go with 2033
notes: basis: "I should go with 2033"; "UPDATE 11 April 2009" paragraph appended to the February 2009 post "Tick, tock, tick, tock…" on his own blog; dated by the update line. Ambiguous field: timeline_year (he keeps 2025 as his straight prediction and offers 2033 as the bias-corrected one he would bet on; the bet is coded).

quote: my prediction for the last 10 years has been for roughly human level AGI in the year 2025 ... my mode is about 2025, my expected value is actually a bit higher at 2028. ... my 90% credibility region, which from my current belief distribution comes out at 2018 to 2036.
claim_summary: Annual review: his prediction for roughly human-level AGI has long been 2025; quantified more carefully, the mode is about 2025, the expected value 2028, and the 90% region 2018 to 2036.
timeline_text: my mode is about 2025, my expected value is actually a bit higher at 2028 ... 90% credibility region ... 2018 to 2036
notes: basis: "my prediction for the last 10 years has been for roughly human level AGI in the year 2025"; His own blog, post "Tick, tock, tick, tock… BING" dated 7 December 2009 on the page. Ambiguous field: timeline_year (he gives a whole distribution; the expected value 2028 is coded as the point year, the mode 2025 and the 90% region are kept in timeline_text). Same post: "computer power is unlikely to be the issue anymore in terms of AGI being possible"; he also predicts sceptics will deny it when it happens. The panel verification used this post as his earliest statement.

quote: More groups will start AGI projects, particularly from 2015 onwards. ... Some of these groups will produce small AGIs that will learn to do some interesting things, but they will be nowhere near human level intelligence. They will, however, be preparing the way for this.
claim_summary: Predictions for the 2010s: more AGI projects, some producing small AGIs, but nowhere near human-level intelligence this decade; they will prepare the way for it.
timeline_text: nowhere near human level intelligence (in the decade to 2020)
notes: basis: "they will be nowhere near human level intelligence"; not_by: 2020; His own blog, post "The teenies" dated 28 December 2009 (predictions for 2010 to 2019). The rejection is only for the decade; his longer forecast in the same month is legg-2009-03. Same post: "Concern at the dangers of artificial intelligence will become less fringe but it won’t go mainstream."

quote: I liked the focus on neuroscience this time. I think it will be a major driving force behind AGI over the next 20 years. ... As I think AGI is approaching, we seriously need much deeper and broader thinking on these topics.
claim_summary: After the 2010 Singularity Summit: neuroscience will drive AGI over the next 20 years; AGI is approaching, so ethics and AGI safety need much deeper thinking.
timeline_text: AGI is approaching
notes: basis: "As I think AGI is approaching"; His own blog, post "Summit 2010" dated 23 August 2010. He proposes "ethics and AGI safety" as the next Summit theme (governance frame). The "next 20 years" is about neuroscience driving AGI work, not an arrival date, so no timeline year is coded.

quote: My longest running prediction, since 1999, has been the time until roughly human level AGI. ... Basically, I gave it a log-normal distribution with a mean of 2028, and a mode of 2025. ... decided to play it safe and keep the prediction unmoved at 2028.
claim_summary: Annual review: his prediction for roughly human-level AGI, held since 1999, is a log-normal distribution with mean 2028 and mode 2025; kept unmoved at 2028 (90% interval about 2018 to 2045).
timeline_text: log-normal distribution with a mean of 2028, and a mode of 2025 ... keep the prediction unmoved at 2028
notes: basis: "keep the prediction unmoved at 2028"; His own blog, post "Goodbye 2010" dated 10 December 2010. Same post corrects the 90% region's upper end to 2045 (lower end 2018). He says progress is "maybe a little faster than I’d expected".

claim_summary: Email Q&A on LessWrong: asked for the years by which he gives 10%, 50% and 90% chance of human-level machine intelligence (assuming no global catastrophe), he answers 2018, 2028, 2050.
timeline_text: 10%/50%/90%: 2018, 2028, 2050 (assuming no global catastrophe)
notes: basis: "2028"; Email interview by XiXiDu (Alexander Kruel), "Q&A with Shane Legg on risks from AI", LessWrong, posted 17 Jun 2011 (read through the greaterwrong.com mirror). The quote is his whole answer to question 1; the question set the 10/50/90 format, so elicitation is survey. This is the "2011 LessWrong" source later press cites for his 50% by 2028.

quote: it’s more likely that it will be the team of humans who understand how it works that will scale it up to something significantly super human, rather than the machine itself. ... Then the machine would be likely to self improve. How fast would that then proceed? Could be very fast, could be impossible
claim_summary: Once human-level AGI exists, a human team will more likely scale it to something significantly superhuman; then the machine would be likely to improve itself, at an unknown speed.
notes: basis: "it’s more likely that it will be the team of humans who understand how it works that will scale it up to something significantly super human"; Same LessWrong email Q&A, answer to question 3 (self-modification to superhuman intelligence within hours, days or five years). One row per capability (A15 ruling 13): this row is the superhuman system; legg-2011-02b is the self-improvement. The self_improvement frame stays on this row because the answer is about getting from human level to superhuman, but the capability here is reached by humans scaling it up, not by the machine improving itself, so the target is superintelligence.

quote: it’s more likely that it will be the team of humans who understand how it works that will scale it up to something significantly super human, rather than the machine itself. ... Then the machine would be likely to self improve. How fast would that then proceed? Could be very fast, could be impossible
claim_summary: After humans scale it up, the machine would be likely to self-improve; how fast is unknown (could be very fast, could be impossible).
timeline_text: How fast would that then proceed? Could be very fast, could be impossible
notes: basis: "Then the machine would be likely to self improve"; Same answer as legg-2011-02a. Ambiguous field: target_capability (a bare "self improve" with no mechanism is coded at the lowest level, si_assist, per the codebook; the speed is explicitly unknown).

quote: When a machine can learn to play a really wide range of games from perceptual stream input and output, and transfer understanding across games, I think we’ll be getting close.
claim_summary: Milestone: when a machine can learn a very wide range of games from perceptual input and transfer understanding across them, human-level machine intelligence will be getting close.
notes: basis: "When a machine can learn to play a really wide range of games"; Same LessWrong email Q&A, answer to question 8 (a milestone after which human-level AI would follow within five years). The question supplied the five-year window; his answer gives the condition only.

quote: I’ve decided to once again leave my prediction for when human level AGI will arrive unchanged. That is, I give it a log-normal distribution with a mean of 2028 and a mode of 2025, under the assumption that nothing crazy happens like a nuclear war. ... I expect to see an impressive proto-AGI within the next 8 years.
claim_summary: Prediction unchanged: human-level AGI log-normal with mean 2028 and mode 2025 (barring something like nuclear war); also an impressive proto-AGI within eight years.
timeline_text: log-normal distribution with a mean of 2028 and a mode of 2025 ... an impressive proto-AGI within the next 8 years
definition_note: proto-AGI: basic vision, sound processing, movement control and language, all learnt rather than preprogrammed, able to solve a range of simple problems including novel ones
notes: basis: "leave my prediction for when human level AGI will arrive unchanged"; His own blog, post "Goodbye 2011, hello 2012" dated 31 December 2011 (the post Dwarkesh Patel read back to him in 2023). The proto-AGI by about 2019 (2011 + 8) is a weaker system than the coded target and has no capability code of its own, so it is kept in timeline_text and definition_note.

quote: I always felt that somewhere around 2030-ish it was about a 50-50 chance. I still feel that seems reasonable. ... maybe there’s some chance that we will have an AGI in a decade. And if not in a decade, well I don’t know, say three decades or so.
claim_summary: DeepMind: The Podcast (season 2, 'The road to AGI'): he has always felt there was about a 50-50 chance of AGI around 2030 and still thinks that reasonable; some chance within a decade, otherwise perhaps three decades.
timeline_text: somewhere around 2030-ish it was about a 50-50 chance ... if not in a decade, well I don't know, say three decades or so
notes: basis: "about a 50-50 chance"; Episode "The road to AGI" (season 2, episode 5) of DeepMind: The Podcast with Hannah Fry, released 15 February 2022 (Apple Podcasts listing); words from a listener's transcription of the episode in a LessWrong post by WilliamKiely (7 Apr 2022), timestamp 5:09, not checked against the audio. Note the year: around 2030 here, against 2028 in his blog and later interviews.

quote: I predicted a 50 percent chance of AGI by 2028. I still believe that today. ... I think that very, very powerful, very intelligent artificial intelligence is coming. I think that this is very, very likely.
claim_summary: On stage with Chris Anderson (TED AI): he still gives a 50% chance of AGI by 2028; very powerful AI is very likely coming (not, he adds, in the next year or two).
timeline_text: a 50 percent chance of AGI by 2028. I still believe that today
notes: basis: "I predicted a 50 percent chance of AGI by 2028. I still believe that today"; TED official transcript; the page gives recordedOn 2023-10-17 (published 2023-12-07), coded at the recording date. Same talk: risks from systems that "potentially have superhuman intelligence" (engineered pathogens, destabilised democracy) alongside large benefits, so consequences mixed.

quote: I think there's a 50% chance that we have AGI by 2028. ... I think it's entirely plausible but I'm not going to be surprised if it doesn't happen by then. ... When I say AGI, I mean a machine that can do the sorts of cognitive things that people can typically do, possibly more.
claim_summary: Dwarkesh Podcast: 50% chance of AGI by 2028, entirely plausible but no surprise if it doesn't happen; AGI means a machine that can do the cognitive things people typically do.
timeline_text: I think there's a 50% chance that we have AGI by 2028
definition_note: a machine that can do the sorts of cognitive things that people can typically do, possibly more
notes: basis: "I think there's a 50% chance that we have AGI by 2028"; Dwarkesh Patel podcast transcript on dwarkesh.com (published time 2023-10-26, timestamp about 0:35). Reason given: training models on more data than a human experiences in a lifetime is now possible ("the first unlocking step"); remaining problems "likely solvable with a number of years of research".

quote: I believe AGI is possible … and I think it’s coming quite soon, ... When it does come, it will be profoundly transformational to society.
claim_summary: At SXSW 2024: AGI is possible and coming quite soon, and will be profoundly transformational; the full spread of practical applications is decades away (reporter's paraphrase).
timeline_text: I think it’s coming quite soon
notes: secondhand; basis: "I think it’s coming quite soon"; AI Business report (published time 2024-03-12) of his remarks "on the sidelines of SXSW 2024", where he spoke with Semafor's Reed Albergotti; month precision because the day of the sideline remarks is not given. "Decades away" for practical applications is the reporter's wording, not coded.

quote: I've been predicting a 50% chance of AGI by 2028 for 20 years.
claim_summary: On X, replying to a critic of AGI hype: he has predicted a 50% chance of AGI by 2028 for 20 years.
timeline_text: a 50% chance of AGI by 2028
notes: basis: "a 50% chance of AGI by 2028"; His X post, a reply to @tmhhope, created 2024-12-13 07:49 UTC (read through X's public embed service). Elicitation unprompted: his own post, though replying to someone.

quote: Is human intelligence going to be the upper limit of what's possible? I think absolutely not. As our understanding of how to build intelligent systems develops, we're going to see these AIs go far beyond human intelligence.
claim_summary: Google DeepMind: The Podcast with Hannah Fry: human intelligence is absolutely not the upper limit; AIs will go far beyond it.
notes: basis: "we're going to see these AIs go far beyond human intelligence"; Episode "The Arrival of AGI with Shane Legg", transcript on spoken.md (third-party; page datePublished 2025-12-11). Only the opening minutes of the transcript were readable; the widely reported "50-50 chance of minimal AGI by 2028" from this episode appears only in summaries (Podwise, all-ai.de) and is not recorded.

quote: Yeah, I think it's a lot more than sparks. ... So my definition of AGI, or sometimes I call minimal AGI, is an artificial agent that can at least do the kinds of cognitive things people can typically do.
claim_summary: Today's AI shows a lot more than sparks of AGI; his 'minimal AGI' is an agent that can at least do the cognitive things people typically do.
definition_note: minimal AGI: an artificial agent that can at least do the kinds of cognitive things people can typically do
notes: Same episode and transcript as legg-2025-01. Asked whether current AIs show "little sparks of being AGI". Ambiguous field: present_capability (more than sparks is a claim of partial presence, not that minimal AGI is here; nothing said about the future in this passage, so endorsement unexpressed).

quote: premature to declare that AGI had been achieved, despite recent claims by executives at Nvidia and OpenAI.
claim_summary: Launching the DeepMind Institute (Financial Times interview): it is premature to declare AGI achieved despite claims by Nvidia and OpenAI executives; he reportedly stays 'comfortable' with 50% for minimal AGI by 2028.
notes: secondhand; AI Weekly (published time 2026-09-16) summarising the Financial Times report as syndicated by Reuters; AI Weekly itself warns these words reach the press as reported, not direct speech. The FT original and the Reuters copy were not readable (paywall; blocked). The 50% by 2028 forecast is reported only in paraphrase ("comfortable"), so no timeline is coded.

quote: No, I won’t dispute the science on any single point, but nonetheless I feel confident in my skepticism. ... More generally, Kurzweil has thirty-four good arguments why his scenario will happen, but only one of those has to fail.
claim_summary: Blog post on Kurzweil's The Singularity Is Near: he won't dispute any single scientific point but is confident in his skepticism; the scenario needs every one of its arguments to hold.
notes: basis: "I feel confident in my skepticism"; His own Marginal Revolution post "Is the Singularity Near?", dated September 21, 2005 on the page; read through the Internet Archive copy. Ambiguous fields: endorsement (skepticism, not a flat "it won't happen"; coded rejects as the nearest code) and target_capability (Kurzweil's Singularity as a whole, read as machine superintelligence). Same post calls Kurzweil "the most important thinker today, if only in expected value terms". Earliest statement in the panel verification.

quote: I believe that machines will never outcompete humans across the board
claim_summary: Writing on what the Singularity would mean for him: machines will never outcompete humans across the board.
notes: secondhand; basis: "machines will never outcompete humans across the board"; Quoted by Arnold Kling in "The Singularity: What's in it for Me?" (EconLog, 2009-10-27), which says "Tyler Cowen tries to answer" and quotes him; Cowen's own piece was not found, so the date is the month of Kling's post. The quote is one sentence; its context is not visible.

quote: the Ray Kurzweil view is within 50 or so years we'll all become computer uploads; our brains will be uploaded into computers. I just find that very, very hard to believe. I think it's a new kind of secular religion. ... I would stress much more that humans can always complement robots.
claim_summary: EconTalk on Average Is Over: Kurzweil's view that within about 50 years we'll all be computer uploads is very hard to believe, a secular religion; humans can always complement robots.
notes: basis: "humans can always complement robots"; EconTalk transcript with Russ Roberts; the transcript gives "Recording date: September 16, 2013" (published 2013-09-30). Ambiguous fields: target_capability and endorsement ("humans can always complement robots" is read as a denial that machines will replace people across the board; the "very hard to believe" is about mind uploading, which has no capability code). Same episode: 50 to 70 years out "much more utopia than dystopia", 20 to 30 years out "much more mixed".

quote: AI represents a truly major, transformational technological advance. ... So when people predict a high degree of existential risk from AGI, I don’t actually think “arguing back” on their chosen terms is the correct response. Radical agnosticism is the correct response, where all specific scenarios are pretty unlikely.
claim_summary: Essay 'Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history': AI is a truly major, transformational advance; the right response to predictions of high existential risk from AGI is radical agnosticism.
notes: Italic marks in the copy removed. Words read in Zvi Mowshowitz's line-by-line reply (published 2023-03-28), which quotes the post verbatim; marginalrevolution.com sits behind a bot check that blocked direct reading; it was not bypassed. Month precision (the reply links the March 2023 post; the post's own day was not visible). Same essay: "Existential risk from AI is indeed a distant possibility, just like every other future you might be trying to imagine"; he supports alignment work and has funded some.

quote: But, the notion of AGI, to me, is not entirely well-defined. ... So, this idea when people say, 'Oh, AGI is X number of years away,' that doesn't make sense to me. If your notion of AGI is a particular kind of smarts, you could argue we're already there.
claim_summary: EconTalk: AGI is not well defined, so 'AGI is X years away' makes no sense to him; on some notions of smarts we could already be there.
notes: EconTalk transcript with Russ Roberts; "Recording date: April 19, 2023" on the page. Ambiguous field: present_capability ("you could argue we're already there" is a hedged claim; he cites GPT-4's measured IQ and test scores).

quote: So, when it comes to AGI [artificial general intelligence] and existential risk, it turns out as best I can ascertain, in the 20 years or so we've been talking about this seriously, there isn't a single model done.
claim_summary: On AGI and existential risk, in some 20 years of serious discussion no one has built a single model of the risk.
notes: Same EconTalk episode as cowen-2023-02 (recording date 2023-04-19). The challenge to build a model of the risk was taken up on LessWrong ("Tyler Cowen's challenge to develop an actual mathematical model"). Same episode: "'here's this big AGI thing, and in 17 years it's going to kill us all,' that is one of the best ways you can imagine not to make progress".

quote: I’m not sure what those numbers going up mean, what a GPT seven would look like, or how much smarter it could get. ... I’m not sure you can just turn up the dial on smarts and have it integrate general relativity and quantum mechanics. ... maybe the universe isn’t that legible
claim_summary: Dwarkesh Podcast: he isn't sure how much smarter later GPTs could get, or that you can turn up the dial on smarts and solve physics; maybe the universe isn't that legible.
notes: basis: "I’m not sure what those numbers going up mean"; Dwarkesh Patel transcript "Hayek, Keynes, & Smith on AI, Animal Spirits, Anarchy, & Growth" (published time 2024-01-31, timestamp about 0:37). Same episode: "Great stagnation is over. We’ll go back to those earlier rates of change" (consequences), and 10% growth for decades "does not seem plausible to me".

quote: Many (not all) insiders now say AGI — artificial general intelligence — stands a good chance of happening in the next few years. AGI is a generative AI model that could, on intellectually oriented tests, outperform human experts on 90% of questions.
claim_summary: Bloomberg column: many insiders now say AGI has a good chance of happening in the next few years; AGI is a model that could outperform human experts on 90% of questions in intellectual tests.
definition_note: a generative AI model that could, on intellectually oriented tests, outperform human experts on 90% of questions
notes: Bloomberg Opinion column "AI Will Transform Philanthropy, Too" (2024-10-14), read in the Bloomberg Law copy, which shows only the opening before a paywall. The "next few years" view is attributed to insiders, not stated as his own, so endorsement is unexpressed. source_type blog is the nearest code for a signed column.

quote: They'll be smart and they'll be conscientious, that I strongly believe. I think they will boost the rate of economic growth by something like half a percentage point a year. Over 30-40 years, that's an enormous difference. It will transform the entire world.
claim_summary: Dwarkesh Podcast (Progress Conference 2024): the AIs will be smart and conscientious, he strongly believes, but will add about half a percentage point a year to growth; over 30 to 40 years that transforms the world.
notes: basis: "They'll be smart and they'll be conscientious, that I strongly believe"; Dwarkesh Patel transcript "The #1 bottleneck to AI progress is humans", recorded at the Progress Conference 2024 (day not given) and published 2025-01-09, coded at the publication date. Ambiguous field: target_capability (replying to a question about AIs that work around the clock; "smart" is not tied to human level). Same interview: "The people who study diffusion of new technologies never think there will be rapid takeoff"; "I see more potential in AI than I did a year ago".

quote: As I said in print, my best estimate is, we get half a percentage point of growth a year. Five percent would be my upper bound.
claim_summary: Conversations with Tyler, with Jack Clark: his best estimate is that AI adds half a percentage point of growth a year, five percent at most.
notes: His own podcast, episode 242 with Jack Clark; the transcript says "Recorded March 28th, 2025". In the transcript the words "my best estimate ... a year" link to his February 2025 post "Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow" (not readable: marginalrevolution.com sits behind a bot check that blocked direct reading; it was not bypassed). Same episode he asks Clark where "AGI" will arrive last and says five well-known people in a green room did not know what AGI meant.

quote: I think it is AGI, seriously. Try asking it lots of questions, and then ask yourself: just how much smarter was I expecting AGI to be? As I’ve argued in the past, AGI, however you define it, is not much of a social event per se. It still will take us a long time to use it properly.
claim_summary: On OpenAI's o3: 'I think it is AGI, seriously'; AGI however defined is not much of a social event, and it will take a long time to use properly.
notes: basis: "I think it is AGI, seriously"; His Marginal Revolution post "o3 and AGI, is April 16th AGI day?" (2025-04-16), read in the verbatim excerpt reposted on Ordinary Times the same day; marginalrevolution.com sits behind a bot check that blocked direct reading; it was not bypassed. The same post (as quoted by Eric Topol and others): "Maybe AGI is like porn — I know it when I see it. And I’ve seen it." Gary Marcus replied the next day. Accepts because the codebook counts "has already happened" as acceptance.

quote: Basically it wipes the floor with the humans, pretty much across the board. ... I don’t mind if you don’t want to call it AGI. And no it doesn’t get everything right, and there are some ways to trick it, typically with quite simple (for humans) questions.
claim_summary: Follow-up post: o3 wipes the floor with humans pretty much across the board; he doesn't mind if you won't call it AGI, and it can still be tricked.
notes: basis: "it wipes the floor with the humans, pretty much across the board"; His post "A note on o3 and AGI" (2025-04-17), read in the verbatim quotation on Bill Benzon's New Savanna blog (2025-04-17, which marks an omission with [...]); marginalrevolution.com sits behind a bot check that blocked direct reading; it was not bypassed.

quote: So I don't care if other people don't call it AGI, but one of the original definitions of AGI was that it would beat most experts most of the time on most matters, say 90% or above, and we're there.
claim_summary: Ground Truths podcast with Eric Topol: one original definition of AGI is beating most experts most of the time on most matters, 90% or more, and we're there.
